That is the share who stopped earlier.

questions.prompt: Two bystanders each independently act with probability 0.5. What is the probability, as a percentage, that at least one acts?
hints: Work out the chance that nobody acts.
Each person fails to act with probability 0.5.
Subtract the chance that nobody acts from 1.
questions.onCorrect: At least one acting is one minus the chance that nobody does: 1 − 0.5², or 0.75.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one person's chance. Two people give two chances.
That is the chance that nobody acts. The question asks about at least one.

questions.prompt: A novice holds one piece per chunk and a master holds five. With a capacity of four chunks, how many more pieces can the master hold?
hints: Find how many pieces each person holds in four chunks.
The novice holds one piece in each chunk.
Subtract the novice's total from the master's.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The master holds 4 × 5 = 20 pieces, the novice 4 × 1 = 4. The difference is 16.

questions.onCorrect: The capacity is the same, but four chunks of five pieces hold far more than four single pieces.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many the master holds. The question asks how many more than the novice.
That is how many the novice holds, not the difference.

questions.prompt: Why is list B so much easier to hold?
hints: Count the digits in each list.
What do you already know about the order 1 to 9?

acceptedIdeas: You know its pattern, so you hold it as one thing, not nine.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: You already know the pattern, so you hold it as one familiar unit instead of nine separate digits.

choices.label: You know its pattern, so you hold it as one thing, not nine.
It has fewer digits.
Its digits are smaller.

questions.onCorrect: Knowledge turns many items into one. You discovered chunking before it had a name.

misconceptions.feedback: Both lists have nine digits, and their size makes no difference to memory.
Both lists have nine digits. The difference is in what you already know.

questions.prompt: What is a chunk?
hints: A chunk depends on what the person knows.

acceptedIdeas: A unit that you already know
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A chunk is a unit already stored in long-term memory, whatever its size.

choices.label: Any single letter or digit
A group of exactly seven items
A unit that you already know

questions.onCorrect: A chunk is whatever you already know as a unit: a letter for one reader, a word for another.

misconceptions.feedback: A single digit is a chunk only if you know nothing that links it to others.
Chunks vary in size. The limit is on how many, not how many items.

questions.prompt: A reader knows the acronyms BBC, NHS and USA. How many chunks is the string BBCNHSUSA for this reader?
hints: Which parts of the string does the reader already know?
Each known acronym is one chunk.
Count the acronyms.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: BBC, NHS and USA are three known units, so three chunks.

questions.onCorrect: Known acronyms make three chunks. Scrambled, the same nine letters would be nine separate chunks.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every letter. The reader holds each known acronym as one unit.
That treats the whole string as one unit. The reader knows three separate acronyms.

questions.prompt: You are repeating a phone number under your breath when someone asks you a question, and you stop rehearsing to answer them. Which part of Baddeley and Hitch's model decided to move your attention?
hints: Which part is a controller rather than a store?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The central executive, which decides what to attend to and when to switch, moved attention from the number to the question.

questions.onCorrect: The central executive made the switch, while the number itself was being held in the phonological loop.

misconceptions.feedback: The sketchpad stores images and positions. It does not direct attention.
The buffer links stored material. Directing attention is another job.
The phonological loop was holding the number. Deciding to stop and attend to the question is the controller's job.

questions.prompt: A gym finds that members who took its fitness programme ended up fitter than members who didn't. Does that show the programme works?
hints: Ask who chose to take the programme.
Would the people who signed up have been the same as the people who didn't, before it began?

acceptedIdeas: Not necessarily: the members who signed up may have been fitter to begin with
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Not necessarily: the members who signed up may have been fitter to begin with

choices.label: Not necessarily: the members who signed up may have been fitter to begin with
Yes, because the people who took it ended up fitter
No, because a gym cannot measure fitness

questions.onCorrect: People who choose a programme can differ from those who don't before it starts, and the gym's records can't show how much of the gap that explains.

misconceptions.feedback: Ending up fitter is what we would see if the programme worked, but also if the keenest and fittest members were the ones who signed up. The result alone can't separate the two.
Fitness can be measured, by a timed run or a heart rate for instance. The difficulty lies in how the two groups came to exist, not in the measuring.

questions.prompt: A disease affects 2 people in every 100. A test detects 90% of the people who have it and wrongly flags 5% of the people who don't. A person tests positive. Roughly how likely is it that they have the disease?
hints: Imagine 1,000 people taking the test and count who ends up with a positive result.
How many of the people who test positive actually have the disease?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 27 in 100: of 67 positives among 1,000 people, 18 have the disease.

choices.label: About 90 in 100
About 27 in 100
About 50 in 100

questions.onCorrect: Counting 1,000 people gives 18 who have the disease and test positive among 67 positives in all, a little over a quarter. We'll build that count step by step.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the test's hit rate, which answers a different question: how often the test is positive among people who have the disease, not how often people who test positive have it.
That would be right only if as many people had the disease as did not, and here far fewer do.

questions.prompt: One group of people saw the wheel stop at 10, and another group saw it stop at 65. Which group gave the higher estimates, typically, of the percentage of African countries in the United Nations?
hints: Think about which direction a number you have just seen would pull your own estimate.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The group that saw 65 gave the higher estimates.

choices.label: The group that saw 10
Neither: the two groups gave the same estimates
The group that saw 65

questions.onCorrect: The group that saw 65 guessed higher, though the wheel was plainly random. The next screens give the numbers.

misconceptions.feedback: The wheel was random, and the pull of a number goes towards that number, so the lower number would pull estimates down and not up.
If a random number could not touch the answer, the two groups would match. They did not, and the gap is what we will measure.

questions.prompt: In a 2013 study, 20 of 24 radiologists searching lung scans for small nodules failed to notice a picture of a gorilla, 48 times the size of a typical nodule, placed in the last scan. Eye-tracking showed that most of those who missed it had looked straight at it. What best explains this?
hints: Ask where the radiologists' attention was while their eyes passed over the gorilla.

acceptedIdeas: Searching for nodules held their attention, and an unexpected object did not capture it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Their attention was on the search for nodules, and a gorilla, which they had no reason to expect, did not draw it away, even when their eyes rested on it.

choices.label: The gorilla was too small or too faint to see clearly
Searching for nodules held their attention, and an unexpected object did not capture it
The radiologists saw the gorilla but forgot it before they were asked

questions.onCorrect: This is inattentional blindness in experts: years of practice at reading scans did not protect them, because looking at something does not guarantee seeing it.

misconceptions.feedback: The gorilla was 48 times the size of a typical nodule, the very thing they were searching for, and most of those who missed it looked straight at it, so its size cannot explain the miss.
Forgetting would not explain why so many experts failed to notice it while their eyes rested on it. What held their attention was the search for nodules, so the gorilla never registered.

questions.prompt: In Watson and Strayer's study, 5 of 200 drivers showed no cost from doing a demanding task while driving. A friend says they drive just as well while on a demanding phone call. What does the study suggest about the claim?
hints: Work out what share of the 200 drivers showed no cost.

acceptedIdeas: It is probably wrong, because only about 1 driver in 40 showed no cost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only 5 of 200 drivers, 2.5%, showed no cost, so for any one driver a cost is far likelier.

choices.label: It is probably wrong, because only about 1 driver in 40 showed no cost
It is probably right, because the study found drivers who showed no cost
The study says nothing about it, because it used a simulator

questions.onCorrect: Supertaskers exist, which matters for the science, but at 2.5% of drivers the sensible expectation for any one person is a cost.

misconceptions.feedback: The study did find such drivers, but only 5 of 200, or 2.5%, so for any one driver the likelier case by far is a cost.
A simulator is not a road, but it let Watson and Strayer compare each driver alone and under a double load, and the great majority did worse when the two were combined.

questions.prompt: Nine digits with no pattern are read out one at a time, and working memory holds about four chunks. What happens when you try to hold all nine?
hints: Ask how many chunks nine separate digits make.

acceptedIdeas: Only about four fit, because each patternless digit takes a chunk of its own
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nine separate digits are nine chunks, so only about four can be held and the rest are lost.

choices.label: Only about four fit, because each patternless digit takes a chunk of its own
All nine fit, because each digit is a small item
All nine fit as three chunks of three, because the mind groups digits by itself

questions.onCorrect: With no pattern to bind them, five of the nine digits have no slot, which is why a long string of random digits slips away.

misconceptions.feedback: The limit counts chunks, however small each item is, and nine separate digits are nine chunks, more than twice what the workspace holds.
Grouping helps only when the groups are something you already know, such as the shape of a phone number, and digits with no pattern give you nothing to group them by.

questions.prompt: A student has a test in a week and a second evening to spend on a chapter she has already read once. Which use of that evening is likely to leave her remembering more of the chapter at the test?
hints: Think about which kind of review did better at the delayed test in Roediger and Karpicke's study.

acceptedIdeas: Closing the book, writing down what she can recall, and then checking it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Practising recall, because retrieval strengthens the memory and its advantage shows at a delayed test.

choices.label: Closing the book, writing down what she can recall, and then checking it
Either, since both spend the same time on the chapter
Reading the chapter through again, since it will feel more familiar

questions.onCorrect: Recall is harder work and may feel less satisfying on the night, but it is the kind of review that is still paying off a week later.

misconceptions.feedback: Rereading makes the chapter feel familiar, but in Roediger and Karpicke's study that fluency did not last, and at the test a week later the students who had practised recall remembered more.
The time is the same, yet trying to bring the ideas to mind strengthens the memory more than looking at them again, which is why recall did better at the delayed test.

questions.prompt: On a fixed-interval 10-second schedule, the first press at least 10 seconds after the previous reward is rewarded. A rat presses the lever every 3 seconds. How often does it earn a reward?
hints: List the times of the presses, 3, 6, 9, 12 and so on, and find the first one at or after 10 seconds.

acceptedIdeas: Every 12 seconds, at the first press after each 10 seconds has passed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The first press at or after 10 seconds comes at 12 seconds, and the clock then restarts, so rewards come every 12 seconds.

choices.label: Every 12 seconds, at the first press after each 10 seconds has passed
Every 10 seconds exactly
Every 3 seconds, on every press after the first 10 seconds

questions.onCorrect: Rewards come at 12, 24, 36, 48 and 60 seconds, five in a minute, because the rat's presses never land exactly on the 10-second mark.

misconceptions.feedback: The interval only makes a reward available, and a press still has to collect it. With presses at 3, 6, 9 and 12 seconds, the first one after 10 seconds comes at 12.
Once a reward is collected the clock starts again, so presses in the next 10 seconds earn nothing, and only the first press after that is rewarded.

questions.prompt: In an illustrative sample of 600 words containing k, 200 start with k and 400 have k as the third letter, yet most people judge that more words start with k. Why?
hints: Try to think of words that start with k, and then of words with k as the third letter.

acceptedIdeas: Memory is searched by first letter, so words starting with k come to mind more easily
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Words that start with k are easy to retrieve because memory is searched by first letter, so they seem more common than they are.

choices.label: People have met more words that start with k than words with k as the third letter
Memory is searched by first letter, so words starting with k come to mind more easily
People guess at random when asked about letters

questions.onCorrect: Judging how common something is by how easily examples come to mind is the availability heuristic, and here ease of recall reflects how memory is searched, not how often the words occur.

misconceptions.feedback: In this sample, words with k as the third letter outnumber those that start with it two to one, so people's reading runs the other way. What differs is how easily each kind comes to mind.
Random guesses would scatter both ways, while people's answers lean the same way, towards the first letter, which points to a systematic cause.

questions.prompt: In Asch's 1956 report, about 37 in every 100 critical answers went along with the wrong majority, while about 75 in every 100 people went along at least once. How can both figures be true?
hints: Ask what each figure counts: answers, or people.

acceptedIdeas: Many people went along on only some of their 12 critical trials, so most people conformed at least once while most answers stayed correct
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One figure counts answers and the other counts people, and most people who conformed did so on only some of their critical trials.

choices.label: Many people went along on only some of their 12 critical trials, so most people conformed at least once while most answers stayed correct
Some people gave more than 12 critical answers each
They come from different experiments, so they cannot both describe one study

questions.onCorrect: Asch read his results both ways for this reason: three quarters of the people conformed at least once, yet roughly two thirds of all critical answers were still correct.

misconceptions.feedback: Both come from the same studies. One counts answers and the other counts people, which is why they differ.
Every participant faced the same 12 critical trials. The figures differ because one is a share of answers and the other a share of people.

flashcards.front: Two measures correlate at r = 0.7. What percentage of their variation do they share?
Towns with more fire engines at a fire record more damage, because larger fires bring more engines and cause more damage. What is fire size in this relationship?
flashcards.back: Fire size is a confound: it drives both the number of engines and the damage.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fire size is a confound: it drives both the number of engines and the damage.

flashcards.front: A therapy group improves by 15 points and a placebo group by 9 points. How many points of improvement are due to the therapy beyond the placebo response?
What procedure gives each participant an equal chance of being placed in any condition of an experiment?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Random assignment.

flashcards.front: Two groups have means 24 and 30, both with standard deviation 12. What is Cohen's d?
Using n ≈ 16/d² per group, how many participants per group are needed to detect d = 0.8 with 80% power?
An observer's hit rate has z = 1.0 and false-alarm rate has z = −0.5. What is d′?
An observer has z(H) = 1.2 and z(FA) = −0.4. What is the criterion location c = −[z(H) + z(FA)]/2?
flashcards.back: c = −(1.2 − 0.4)/2 = −0.4, a slight bias towards yes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: c = −(1.2 − 0.4)/2 = −0.4, a slight bias towards yes.

flashcards.front: Each trial takes 700 ms and each change of task adds 250 ms. How long does the sequence ABBA take, in milliseconds?
What name is given to the phenomenon in which people counting basketball passes miss a person in a gorilla suit?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inattentional blindness.

flashcards.front: Two independent cues have standard deviations of 6 and 8. What is the standard deviation of their reliability-weighted combination?
Cue A reads 20 with SD 3 and cue B reads 30 with SD 3. What is the reliability-weighted combined estimate?
Someone groups 15 letters into 5 familiar words. Against a capacity of 4 chunks, how many chunks over the limit are they?
Which component of Baddeley and Hitch's working-memory model directs attention and coordinates the other parts?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The central executive.

flashcards.front: Using R = 1/(1 + t/9S) with stability S = 3 days, what percentage recall is predicted 9 days later?
A memory has stability 8 days, and a successful review multiplies stability by 2.5. What is the new stability in days?
Rescorla–Wagner with rate 0.4, maximum 1 and V starting at 0: what is V after two paired trials?
Which reinforcement schedule produces behaviour that is most resistant to extinction?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The variable-ratio schedule.

flashcards.front: 1,000 people are screened for a condition that 2% have. The test misses no cases but gives false positives for 5% of people without it. How many false positives are there?
A screening programme finds 12 true positives and 36 false positives. What percentage of positive results are correct?
Mould on a loaf doubles its area every day and covers the whole loaf on day 12. On which day did it cover half the loaf?
flashcards.back: Doubling means it was half the size one day earlier: day 11.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Doubling means it was half the size one day earlier: day 11.

flashcards.front: Anchors of 10 and 60 produce median estimates of 30 and 40. What is the anchoring index?
In a conformity study, 21 of 60 critical answers follow the wrong majority. What percentage conformed?
Two bystanders each independently act with probability 0.4. What is the probability, as a percentage, that at least one acts?

A 16-digit card number is printed in groups of four. If each group becomes one chunk, how many chunks must be held? 16 digits / 4 per group = 4 chunks.
What is the strategy of organising items into meaningful groups so more fits in short-term memory called? Chunking: grouping items into units already known from long-term memory.

A novice holds one piece per chunk and a master holds five. With a capacity of four chunks, how many more pieces can the master hold? The master holds 4 × 5 = 20 pieces, the novice 4 × 1 = 4. The difference is 16.
How many digits exceed the limit? Nine chunks against a capacity of four leaves 9 − 4 = 5 beyond the limit.
A reader knows the acronyms BBC, NHS and USA. How many chunks is the string BBCNHSUSA for this reader? BBC, NHS and USA are three known units, so three chunks.
A chess master recalls a 20-piece position as 4 chunks. On average, how many pieces are in each chunk? 20 pieces / 4 chunks = 5 pieces a chunk.
Switching attention from rehearsing a number to answering a question is the work of the central executive.

Lists of similar-sounding words are harder to recall in order. Which part of Baddeley and Hitch's working-memory model does this point to? The phonological loop stores speech-based codes, so similar sounds interfere with one another.
Someone groups 15 letters into 5 familiar words. Against a capacity of 4 chunks, how many chunks over the limit are they? 5 chunks − 4 = 1 over the limit.
Which component of Baddeley and Hitch's working-memory model directs attention and coordinates the other parts? The central executive.
Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve shows steep early loss then slower loss; Murre and Dros (2015) replicated the procedure with one volunteer and found a similar curve.
In the FSRS model stability S is the interval at which predicted recall falls to 90%; the FSRS-4 form is R = 1/(1 + t/9S), and later versions have a flatter tail.

56% recall after practising recall against 42% after rereading is a 14-point gap (illustrative values in the pattern of the finding).
A memory has stability S = 4 days. Using R = 1/(1 + t/9S), what percentage recall is predicted 108 days after learning? 9S = 36; t/9S = 108/36 = 3; R = 1/(1 + 3) = 25%.
Studying in short sessions spread over days, rather than one long session, is called what kind of practice? Distributed, or spaced, practice.

A memory has stability 6 days. A successful review multiplies stability by 3. How many days after that review is the card next due, when recall falls to 90%? The new stability is 6 × 3 = 18 days, and a card is due when recall falls to 90%, which is S days after the review.
What percentage recall does the curve predict 90 days after learning? t/9S = 90/90 = 1, so R = 1/(1 + 1) = 0.5, or 50%.
Why does a larger stability slow forgetting? A larger S makes 9S bigger, so t ÷ 9S grows slowly and recall stays high longer.
What percentage recall is predicted 13.5 days after that review? 9S = 54; t/9S = 13.5/54 = 0.25; R = 1/1.25 = 0.8, or 80%.

A card has stability 8 days. If reviews are scheduled for when predicted recall falls to 90%, how many days after its last review is it due? Stability is defined as the interval at which predicted recall reaches 90%, so the card is due in 8 days.

A week after studying, students who practised recall remembered 56% of idea units and students who reread remembered 42%. How many percentage points higher was recall practice? 56 − 42 = 14 percentage points.
Using R = 1/(1 + t/9S) with stability S = 3 days, what percentage recall is predicted 9 days later? t/9S = 9/27 = 1/3; R = 1/(4/3) = 0.75, or 75%.
A memory has stability 8 days, and a successful review multiplies stability by 2.5. What is the new stability in days? 8 × 2.5 = 20 days.
In classical conditioning a neutral stimulus paired with an unconditioned stimulus comes to elicit a conditioned response; Pavlov's dogs salivated to a conditioned stimulus.
Rescorla and Wagner (1972): associative strength changes on each trial by the rate times the difference between the maximum and the current strength.
With rate 0.3 and maximum 1, V is 0.3 after one pairing and 0.3 + 0.3 x 0.7 = 0.51 after two.

Extinction is the weakening of a conditioned response when the conditioned stimulus is no longer followed by the unconditioned stimulus, and spontaneous recovery is its partial return after a rest; in the Rescorla-Wagner rule the maximum is 0 on cue-alone trials.
With V = 0.5, rate 0.2 and maximum 0, the change is 0.2 x (0 - 0.5) = -0.1, so V becomes 0.4.
With rate 0.5 the strength is 0.5, 0.75, then 0.75 + 0.5 x (0 - 0.75) = 0.375.

Operant conditioning changes behaviour by its consequences: reinforcement increases and punishment decreases behaviour, and positive and negative mean adding or removing a stimulus; Thorndike's law of effect preceded Skinner's work.
Adding a pleasant consequence that raises a behaviour is positive reinforcement.

Fixed-ratio, variable-ratio, fixed-interval and variable-interval schedules produce different response patterns, with variable-ratio behaviour the most resistant to extinction; Ferster and Skinner published their schedules research in 1957.
On a fixed-ratio 5 schedule, 30 responses earn 6 rewards.
On a fixed-interval 10 s schedule with a response every 3 s, rewarded responses fall at 12, 24, 36, 48 and 60 s: five rewards.
A slot machine pays out after an unpredictable number of plays, averaging one win in twenty. Which reinforcement schedule is this? Variable ratio: rewards follow an unpredictable number of responses.

A child's screen time is taken away after they hit a sibling, and the hitting becomes less frequent. Which consequence is this? Something pleasant is removed (negative) and the behaviour decreases (punishment).
The rate is 0.6, the maximum is 1 and V starts at 0. What is V after two pairings? Trial 1: V = 0.6. Trial 2: V = 0.6 + 0.6 × (1 − 0.6) = 0.6 + 0.24 = 0.84.
What is V after two pairings? Trial 1: V = 0 + 0.3 × 1 = 0.3. Trial 2: V = 0.3 + 0.3 × (1 − 0.3) = 0.51.
Why does V fall on a bell-alone trial? Without food the bell predicts nothing, so the maximum is 0 and the change is negative.
Starting from V = 0, what is the final V? Pairings: 0.5, then 0.75. Alone: 0.75 + 0.5 × (0 − 0.75) = 0.375.
Praise follows a pupil raising a hand, and hand-raising becomes more frequent. Is this positive or negative reinforcement? Positive reinforcement: praise is added and the behaviour rises.
It makes 30 pecks. How many rewards does it earn? Every fifth response is rewarded: 30/5 = 6.

On a fixed-interval 10-second schedule, a rat presses every 3 seconds for 60 seconds. The first press at least 10 s after the previous reward is rewarded. How many rewards does it earn? Rewarded presses fall at 12, 24, 36, 48 and 60 s: five rewards.
Rescorla–Wagner with rate 0.4, maximum 1 and V starting at 0: what is V after two paired trials? 0.4, then 0.4 + 0.4 × 0.6 = 0.64.
Which reinforcement schedule produces behaviour that is most resistant to extinction? The variable-ratio schedule.
Counting people gives natural frequencies: of 1,000 people with a base rate of 2%, 20 have the disease and 980 do not.
With a base rate of 2%, a 90% hit rate and a 5% false-alarm rate, 18 true positives and 49 false positives give 18 of 67 positives (about 27%) correct.
With a 1% base rate and a 10% false-alarm rate, 99 of 990 people without the disease are flagged.

Tversky and Kahneman (1974) report that people judging whether a described man was an engineer or a lawyer gave nearly the same probabilities whether the group was 30 engineers and 70 lawyers or the reverse, neglecting the base rate.
The positive predictive value is true positives divided by all positives.
With 500 people, a 10% base rate, 60% hit rate and 20% false-alarm rate, 30 of 120 positives are true (25%).
With a 1% base rate, 90% hit rate and 10% false-alarm rate, 9 of 108 positives are true (8.3%).
The same test (50% hit rate, 5% false-alarm rate) gives a positive predictive value of 10/59 (17%) at a 2% base rate and 100/140 (71%) at a 20% base rate.
With a 10% base rate, 90 true positives and 90 false positives make half of positive results true.
With 20% blue cabs and a 75%-accurate witness, 150 of 350 'blue' calls are correct (42.9%); the cab puzzle was made famous by Kahneman and Tversky with other numbers.

2,000 people are tested for a condition that 5% have. The test detects 80% of cases and gives false positives for 10% of people without it. How many people test positive in total? 100 have it, 80 test positive; 1,900 do not, 190 test positive; 80 + 190 = 270.

A doctor judges a positive result from a 90%-accurate test as 90% likely to be right, ignoring that the disease is rare. What is this error called? Base-rate neglect: the prior frequency of the condition is ignored.

Of 1,000 people, 5% have a condition. The test flags 80% of cases and 10% of people without it. What percentage of positive results are correct? Give one decimal place. 50 have it and 40 test positive; 950 do not and 95 test positive. 40 ÷ 135 = 0.296, or 29.6%.
Counting 1,000 people gives 18 who have the disease and test positive among 67 positives in all, a little over a quarter. We'll build that count step by step.
How many false positives are there? 1,000 − 10 = 990 people do not have the disease; 10% of 990 = 99 false positives.
Why divide by all 120 positives, not by the 50 people who have the disease? The question is about someone who tested positive, so the flagged group is the whole of the comparison.
What is the probability, as a percentage, that a person who tests positive has the disease? Give one decimal place. 9/(9 + 99) = 9/108 = 0.0833, or 8.3%.
What percentage of positive results are true positives? 100 have it and 90 test positive; 900 do not and 90 test positive; 90/180 = 50%.

20% of a city's cabs are blue. A witness who names colours correctly 75% of the time says the cab was blue. What is the probability, as a percentage, that it was blue? Give one decimal place. Per 1,000 cabs: 150 blue cabs called blue and 200 green cabs called blue; 150/350 = 42.9%.

1,000 people are screened for a condition that 2% have. The test misses no cases but gives false positives for 5% of people without it. How many false positives are there? 980 do not have it; 5% of 980 = 49.
A screening programme finds 12 true positives and 36 false positives. What percentage of positive results are correct? 12/(12 + 36) = 12/48 = 25%.

In Tversky and Kahneman (1974), a wheel of fortune stopped at 10 or 65 and participants then estimated the percentage of African countries in the United Nations; estimates were pulled towards the number.
Median estimates were 25% after the anchor 10 and 45% after 65, a gap of 20 percentage points.
The anchoring index (Jacowitz and Kahneman, 1995) is the difference in median estimates divided by the difference in anchors: 20/55 = 0.36 for the wheel experiment.

200 of 600 words is 33.3% (illustrative counts).
Frederick (2005) used problems with a tempting wrong quick answer to measure cognitive reflection; System 1 and System 2 are labels from Stanovich and West popularised by Kahneman.
Ball x and bat x + 100p give 2x + 100 = 110, so the ball costs 5p, not the intuitive 10p.
Anchors of 100 and 500 produce median estimates of 220 and 340. What is the anchoring index? (340 − 220)/(500 − 100) = 120/400 = 0.3.

After several news reports of shark attacks, a swimmer judges sharks a bigger risk than drowning. Judging frequency by how easily examples come to mind is which heuristic? The availability heuristic: vivid, easily recalled cases feel common.
A pen and a notebook cost £2.20 together. The notebook costs £2.00 more than the pen. How much does the pen cost, in pence? Pen x, notebook x + 200: 2x + 200 = 220, so x = 10p.
The group that saw 65 guessed higher, though the wheel was plainly random. The next screens give the numbers.
By how many percentage points did the medians differ? 45 − 25 = 20 percentage points.
What does an index of 0.35 say about the anchors? An index between 0 and 1 shows how far the estimates moved, as a share of the anchors' gap.
What is the anchoring index, (difference in medians) ÷ (difference in anchors)? (59 − 35)/(80 − 20) = 24/60 = 0.4.

In a sample of 600 English words containing k, 200 start with k and 400 have k as the third letter. What percentage start with k? Give one decimal place. 200/600 = 0.333, or 33.3%: words with k third are twice as common, though harder to recall.
How much does the ball cost, in pence? Ball x, bat x + 100p: 2x + 100 = 110, so x = 5p. The intuitive 10p would make the total £1.20.
Mould on a loaf doubles its area every day and covers the whole loaf on day 12. On which day did it cover half the loaf? Doubling means it was half the size one day earlier: day 11.
Anchors of 10 and 60 produce median estimates of 30 and 40. What is the anchoring index? (40 − 30)/(60 − 10) = 10/50 = 0.2.
Conformity is changing behaviour or belief to match a group; confederates are helpers of the experimenter.
72 conforming answers out of 18 x 12 = 216 is 33.3% (illustrative counts).
